# CloudBitmaps

> Distributed, cloud-native Roaring Bitmaps. Query and intersect billion-scale integer sets straight out of
> object storage — a bounded RAM cache over immutable `.crbm` generations in your own bucket — at a fraction
> of an always-on cache, with the familiar bitmap API: `has`, `count`, `iterate`, `intersect`, `union`,
> `andNot`.

CloudBitmaps maps each 16-bit Roaring chunk onto pluggable cloud storage: a hot in-process LRU over a cold
tier of write-once `.crbm` generations, with one small registry row per segment saying which generation is
current. The distinguishing capability is **serverless chunk-skipping intersection**: `A ∩ B` fetches only the
chunks that can possibly contribute, so intersecting two 2,000,000-id segments touches only the shared chunks,
and `count()` on a published segment does zero payload reads.

Install `@cloudbitmaps/roaring` — `@cloudbitmaps/core` (the codec-agnostic engine plus all the storage
drivers) arrives transitively. Five storage backends: S3, GCS, Azure Blob and DynamoDB as optional-peer
subpaths, plus the local filesystem in the main entry.

## How data gets in

Only by loading a whole new generation. `bulkLoadCrbmGeneration(cold, {segment, generation}, ids, {registry})`
streams an array, a Set or an async cursor into one immutable object and then advances the registry pointer,
forward-only. Nothing mutates a stored bitmap, so a crash before the publish leaves the previous generation
authoritative, a rerun is idempotent, and there is no partially-visible write. There is no add, addMany,
remove or claimMany, and no store.compact. `intersectInto`/`unionInto`/`andNotInto` use the same protocol,
publishing their result as a new generation of the destination segment.

Reads see one whole, checksum-verified generation: has (hot cache, else one ranged GET), count (exact, summed
from the .crbm index with zero payload reads), iterate, and intersect/union/andNot — the chunk-skipping
composites, with `exclude` suppression folded into the same pass.

## Measured, not modelled

Benchmarked against real S3 + DynamoDB in us-east-1 — not an emulator — with the request counts read off the
AWS SDK layer: $0.14 per million count()s and $5.88 per million segment publishes, against an
always-on Redis-HA line of $346/month standing, and $0.03/month for 1.2 GiB of segments at rest. One crossover
is published: past 329.15 sustained reads a second, with every read missing the hot cache, metered GETs pass
the standing node — a warmer cache moves that line up.

## Coming from Redis bitmaps

A durable home for set-shaped work — audiences, dedup, suppression, membership, eligibility — where the sets
are large, mostly read, must survive a restart, and are computed in batches upstream. The read side maps
one-for-one: GETBIT/BITCOUNT become has/count, BITOP AND/OR/DIFF become intersect/union/andNot, and intersect
skips the chunks that cannot contribute. You are not giving up the bitmap either: past 4,096 ids in a
65,536-id chunk (6.25% of it) Roaring stores that chunk as a flat bit array, byte for byte what a Redis bitmap
holds.

Not a drop-in replacement, and the two limits are load-bearing rather than footnotes:

1. No per-id write, and that is the difference. SETBIT has no equivalent: a segment changes only by publishing
   a new generation, so a SETBIT loop has nothing to port to. If the set is defined by a query, run the query
   and load the result; if it is defined by events arriving one at a time, accumulate them where they arrive
   (Redis is genuinely good at that) and load the set on a cadence. A load bills per object, not per id — ten
   million ids are a handful of PUTs. Removing one id everywhere is a compliance operation (eraseSubject, a
   generation rewrite), not a hot-path verb.
2. No addressable-bit surface. BITPOS, BITFIELD, byte-range BITCOUNT and BITOP NOT have no equivalent — this is
   a set of ids, not a positional bit buffer, and NOT has no bounded universe to complement against. The raw
   bytes are not interoperable either: a .crbm object is not a flat bit array, and raw bit-position import is
   not built.

Retention is per segment and built in: setRetention(ref, {expiresAt}) records when a segment becomes eligible
for retirement, and retireExpired() is the sweep that acts on it, retiring each expired segment through
dropSegment. The expiry is an absolute instant the writer sets, not a duration derived from anything observed,
because every load rewrites the basis such a duration would use. The sweep is a function you schedule -- this
library starts no timer, so the same code behaves identically in a Lambda, an edge isolate and a long-running
server. There is no per-id TTL: a bitmap stores ids, not timestamps, and a per-id timestamp costs more than the
compression saves.

## No background process, and nothing to seed

There is no daemon, no compaction pass and no lifecycle worker. A segment exists once a generation has been
loaded into it, and the only scheduled work is the retention sweep above (plus gcOrphanGenerations, which never
touches the current generation, if you want superseded ones collected sooner). Compliance is built in:
subjectReport (Art. 15), eraseSubject (Art. 17 -- a generation rewrite that deletes the generation holding the
bit, so it is physically gone from the bucket when the call returns), destroySegment/eraseNamespace
(crypto-shred), dropSegment, checkConsistency, and exportSegments -- eject every segment to portable roaring or
ndjson, which is the exit path.

## When NOT to use it

If you need a sub-millisecond p99 on a working set that fits a bounded hot cache, use Redis: a check that
misses the hot cache costs a ranged GET against object storage, where an in-process RAM store costs a memory
read. CloudBitmaps is for sets that are large, mostly read, and shouldn't cost $346/month to keep warm.
In-region latency is not yet calibrated and no in-region figure is published.

## Status

v0.9.0, Apache-2.0, published tokenlessly with SLSA build provenance. Pre-1.0: breaking changes are possible
in a minor bump until the .crbm format freezes at 1.0.
